title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Introduction
content: Breast milk production begins in significant amounts between 2 and 4 days after birth, commonly described as the milk “coming in.” This process marks the transition from colostrum, the nutrient-rich early milk, to mature breast milk. Breast milk remains the optimal source of nutrition for infants, uniquely tailored to meet all nutritional, developmental, and immunological needs during early life. It supplies essential macronutrients, micronutrients, growth factors, hormones, and antibodies required for growth and protection against infection.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Introduction
content: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, followed by continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods up to 2 years of age or beyond [WHO, 2025 https://www.who.int/health-topics/breastfeeding#tab=tab_1 ; PAHO, 2025 https://www.paho.org/en/topics/breastfeeding-and-complementary-feeding ]. Current global estimates show that approximately 48% of infants younger than 6 months are exclusively breastfed, approaching the World Health Assembly’s 2025 target of 50%. [1]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Introduction
content: Recent studies have highlighted that breast milk composition is far more dynamic than previously thought, influenced by maternal health, diet, circadian rhythm, and environmental factors. For instance, the bioactive components and microbiome of breast milk fluctuate between day and night, modulating the infant’s metabolism and immune function. [2] Genetic factors also play an emerging role in lactation variability; new research has identified gene expression patterns linked to milk production capacity. [3]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Introduction
content: Beyond its nutritional function, breastfeeding has been associated with long-term health benefits for both the mother and child. Studies suggest that breastfeeding stimulates immune cell activity that may protect mothers against breast cancer, while infants benefit from enhanced immune regulation and neurodevelopmental outcomes. [4] Furthermore, advancements in molecular biology have revealed that breast milk contains diverse cellular populations, including immune and stem cells, reflecting its complex physiological and regenerative nature. [5]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Introduction
content: Collectively, these findings reinforce that breast milk is a living, adaptive biological fluid central to early human development. Ongoing global initiatives such as the WHO Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative and the Global Breastfeeding Collective continue to advocate for policies and programs that protect, promote, and support breastfeeding as a cornerstone of maternal and child health.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Issues of Concern
content: In many parts of the world, formula feeding has become increasingly common, often replacing breast milk as the preferred choice. However, growing evidence continues to demonstrate the significant disadvantages of formula and bottle feeding compared with breastfeeding. Formula feeding is associated with a higher risk of infections, oral malocclusion, obesity, and altered oxygenation and thermoregulation in infants. It also disrupts the development of a healthy gut microbiota, with long-term effects on immunity and metabolism. [6]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Issues of Concern
content: Vitamin D: VLBW or breastfed infants should receive 400–1000 IU vitamin D per day from birth until 12 months of age. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends starting supplementation soon after birth for all breastfed infants to prevent rickets and ensure adequate bone development. [7] Calcium and Phosphorus: Infants fed breast milk require additional calcium (120–140 mg/kg/day) and phosphorus (60–90 mg/kg/day) during the first month of life. Iron: Iron supplementation of 2–4 mg/kg/day is needed for VLBW infants fed breast milk until at least 6 months of age. For preterm infants born before 35 weeks’ gestation, 0.2 mL/kg/dose every 12 hours from 4 weeks of age until 6 months is recommended. Vitamin K: Because breast milk contains very low levels of vitamin K, all newborns should receive vitamin K at birth to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Issues of Concern
content: The WHO and the AAP strongly recommend the use of pasteurized donor human milk (PDHM) for preterm and low-birth-weight infants if the mother’s milk is unavailable. PDHM significantly reduces the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and other severe complications compared with formula feeding. [8] Donor milk should always be pasteurized and fortified to meet the nutritional needs of premature infants.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Issues of Concern
content: In addition, studies continue to demonstrate the importance of maternal nutrition. For infants with anemia, iron supplementation directly given to the infant is effective, but improving the mother’s iron intake through iron-rich foods or supplements also helps boost the nutrient content of breast milk. Maternal vitamin D supplementation of 2000 IU/day can raise breast milk vitamin D concentrations to support infant needs.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Issues of Concern
content: Overall, maintaining breastfeeding even alongside necessary supplementation in high-risk infants provides unmatched immunological and developmental advantages. Health systems and policymakers should continue to promote access to donor milk, clinical support for breastfeeding mothers, and evidence-based supplementation protocols to ensure optimal infant growth and long-term health worldwide.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level
content: During the first week after childbirth, the mother secretes colostrum, a thick, yellow, nutrient-rich liquid packed with antibodies and immune cells. Between days 7 and 14, this transitions into transitional milk, a blend of colostrum and mature milk. After 2 weeks, mature milk is established and secreted. Recent studies confirm that milk composition continues to evolve months after birth as maternal and infant needs change, underscoring breast milk’s dynamic and adaptive nature. [5]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level
content: Breast milk can be visually divided into 2 parts during each feeding: foremilk, which is bluish-grey and lower in fat, and hindmilk, which is creamy white and rich in fat. This shift in composition ensures that infants receive both hydration and energy-dense nutrition. Research shows that fat and cell content in milk peak about 30 minutes after feeding, reflecting direct responses to breast emptying and milk synthesis. [9]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level
content: Milk composition varies among mothers and even within the same individual, depending on maternal health, nutritional status, genetics, environmental exposures, gestational age, and the infant’s stage of growth. [10]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level
content: On average, breast milk contains approximately 87% water, 3% to 5% fat, 6.9% to 7.2% lactose, and 0.8% to 0.9% protein, along with vitamins, minerals, hormones, immune factors, and thousands of bioactive molecules (Nature Pediatric Research, 2025). It provides 60-75 kcal/100 mL. Colostrum is higher in protein and immunoglobulins, while mature milk contains more carbohydrates.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level -- Fats
content: The fat content of breast milk varies widely, influenced by maternal diet, health, and lactation stage. Recent systematic reviews confirm that omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid concentrations reflect maternal intake and metabolic conditions. [10] Triglycerides form the bulk of milk lipids, with saturated fatty acids making up nearly 50%, including about 23% palmitic acid. Breast milk also provides essential fatty acids, such as linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids, which are converted to arachidonic acid (AA), eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), all of which are critical for brain and retinal development.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level -- Carbohydrates
content: Human milk primarily contains lactose, which helps maintain osmotic balance and supports calcium absorption. More than 200 distinct oligosaccharides have now been identified, far exceeding earlier estimates, acting as natural prebiotics that support beneficial gut bacteria and immune defense. [11] Their composition changes with the lactation stage and maternal genetic factors known as “secretor” status.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level -- Proteins
content: The protein content of human milk decreases as lactation progresses, ranging from 1.4–1.6 g/100 mL in early lactation to about 0.7–0.8 g/100 mL after 6 months. The major proteins are whey and casein, with the whey/casein ratio shifting from 80/20 in early lactation to about 50/50 later. Key functional proteins include alpha-lactalbumin, lysozyme, lactoferrin, and immunoglobulin A (IgA)—all essential for digestion, nutrient transport, and immune defense. Glutamine remains the most abundant amino acid, up to 20 times higher in mature milk than in colostrum. Lactocytes, the milk-producing epithelial cells, adjust their gene expression over time in response to hormonal and environmental factors, accounting for these variations in composition.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level -- Vitamins and Minerals
content: Breast milk naturally contains sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, chlorine, iron, copper, and zinc, though in modest concentrations; their bioavailability is exceptionally high. The levels of these trace elements fluctuate depending on maternal health and diet. Vitamins D and K are present in low amounts; hence, both maternal supplementation and newborn prophylaxis remain vital.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Cellular Level -- Bioactive Substances
content: Breast milk is biologically active, containing white blood cells, antibodies (IgA, IgG, IgM), cytokines, chemokines, hormones, enzymes, and growth factors. Epidermal growth factor (EGF) promotes intestinal maturation, while secretory IgA protects the infant’s mucosal surfaces by neutralizing pathogens. Breast milk also includes signaling molecules that influence infant immune programming and neurodevelopment.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Development
content: Breast development begins around the sixth week of embryonic life, with the appearance of a linear ridge known as the milk line or mammary ridge along the ventral surface of the embryo. These paired epithelial thickenings extend from the axilla to the groin. By the eighth week, proliferation within the pectoral region forms the primary mammary bud, which invades the underlying mesenchyme. Most of the ridge regresses except for the pectoral portion, which gives rise to the definitive mammary gland. [12]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Development
content: During the late first and second trimesters, the primary bud elongates and gives rise to secondary epithelial sprouts, which branch and canalize to form lactiferous ducts. By approximately 6 months of gestation, the fundamental architecture of the gland, including the ductal tree and the initial lobular framework, is established. Differentiation of myoepithelial cells from the basal layer occurs in this period, positioning these contractile cells around developing alveoli and ducts.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Development
content: Beyond 31 weeks of gestation, the distal ducts expand into bulbous outpouchings that form the papillary and areolar complexes. Occlusion of the papillary lumen results in the formation of the nipple-areola complex, which becomes fully developed at birth. At this stage, the breast is structurally complete but functionally inactive until puberty and pregnancy.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Development
content: The postnatal breast contains both glandular and adipose tissue, supported by Cooper’s ligaments, which maintain the breast’s structural integrity. The glandular tissue consists of lobes, subdivided into lobules, each containing clusters of alveoli, the milk-producing units lined by secretory epithelial cells. These alveoli are surrounded by myoepithelial cells that contract in response to oxytocin, propelling milk through ducts toward the nipple. Ducts converge into lactiferous sinuses beneath the areola before narrowing to exit through openings on the nipple surface. The areola also contains Montgomery glands, which secrete a lubricating fluid that protects the nipple and releases scent cues that help guide the infant to the breast.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Development
content: During pregnancy, the mother undergoes stage II mammogenesis under the influence of progesterone, prolactin, and human chorionic gonadotropin. These hormones stimulate the formation of type III lobules, consisting of enlarged alveoli with abundant epithelial cells and secretory acini. In late pregnancy, hypertrophic alveoli undergo partial atrophy, creating space for colostrum accumulation in preparation for lactation. [13]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Organ Systems Involved
content: The mammary glands, the anterior pituitary gland, and the posterior pituitary gland are the organs and structures involved in breast milk formation. The individual roles of those organs are discussed below.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Function
content: By the third day postpartum, the average amount of breast milk consumed by an infant is approximately 300 to 400 mL per 24 hours, increasing to 500 to 800 mL by the fifth day. Over the first 6 months, milk intake typically averages around 800 mL per day. Breastfed infants who feed according to their appetite generally empty only about 70% of the available milk during nursing sessions, highlighting the dynamic nature of milk storage and flow.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Function
content: The composition of breast milk changes over time to meet the specific needs of the growing infant. The initial milk, called foremilk, satisfies the baby's thirst due to its higher water content. As the feeding progresses, the hindmilk provides more fat, offering calorie-dense nutrition essential for infant energy requirements. Breast milk also plays a critical role in postnatal intestinal function, immune system development (ontogeny), and brain growth.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Function
content: Extensive research confirms breast milk's superiority over formula and animal milk in protecting against a broad range of infections, including otitis media, lower respiratory tract infections, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bronchiolitis, sudden infant death syndrome, and necrotizing enterocolitis. Breastfeeding is also associated with reduced risks of chronic diseases such as obesity, allergies, asthma, eczema, celiac disease, Crohn disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and certain leukemias.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Function
content: The fat content in breast milk is vital for regulating growth, inflammatory responses, immune function, vision, cognitive development, and motor skills. Key fatty acids like docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and arachidonic acid are crucial for nerve cell differentiation and active synapse development; notably, these fatty acids are absent in other types of milk. [10] Lactose facilitates the absorption of minerals and calcium, while specific carbohydrates foster the growth of beneficial lactobacilli in the gut, which are essential for maintaining a healthy intestinal flora.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Function
content: Proteins in breast milk are lower than in animal milk, as excess protein can overload immature kidneys due to nitrogen waste. Breast milk contains a higher proportion of whey proteins, which are easier to digest for newborns compared to the predominantly casein-based proteins in cow's milk formulas. Whey proteins provide immune support, for example, IgA coats and protects the gut, while lactoferrin and lysozymes defend against bacterial pathogens. The protein-rich peptide (PRP) supports thymus activity to regulate immune responses and mitigate allergies and autoimmune conditions. Alpha-lactalbumin is essential for lactose synthesis and calcium/zinc binding, and bile-salt-stimulated lipase aids fat digestion in the infant's small intestine, unlike artificial milk fat, which is only partially digested. Glutamine provides key metabolic substrates and plays a role in neurotransmission in the gut and brain.

content: Vitamins and minerals in breast milk are critical for newborn enzymatic functions and molecular synthesis. Vitamins D and K are absent and require supplementation. Iron is also essential for preventing anemia in infants.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Function
content: Colostrum, secreted during the first 2 to 3 days postpartum in small quantities (about 30–60 mL/day), is especially rich in white blood cells and antibodies, mainly IgA, providing early protection against pathogens such as providing early protection against pathogens such as E. coli , Salmonella , RSV, Candida , Streptococcus , Staphylococcus , Cryptosporidium , and Helicobacter pylori . It contains higher levels of protein, minerals, and fat-soluble vitamins A, E, and K compared to mature milk. Vitamin A plays a key role in eye protection and in the formation of epithelial tissue. Colostrum also carries abundant growth factors, including insulin-like growth factors 1 and 2 and EGF, which promote intestinal lining maturation. Maternal conditions like eclampsia, diabetes, or anemia may influence colostrum composition. Feeding newborns exclusively with colostrum is crucial in the early postnatal period.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Mechanism
content: A neonate typically breastfeeds every 1 to 3 hours for about 10 to 20 minutes per session early on. As the infant grows, the frequency and duration of feeding decrease because the baby can extract more milk in less time. This natural progression aligns with the infant’s developmental capabilities and nutritional needs [CDC, 2025 https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/breastfeeding/how-much-and-how-often.html ].

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Mechanism
content: Two key hormones regulate breast milk production and ejection: prolactin and oxytocin. Prolactin stimulates milk synthesis by acting on the mammary epithelial cells. Its levels rise during pregnancy, promoting the proliferation of mammary tissue. However, high levels of progesterone and estrogen inhibit milk secretion despite elevated prolactin. After placental delivery, the drop in these hormones removes this inhibition, allowing prolactin to trigger milk production. Prolactin secretion is stimulated by infant suckling at the nipple, reaching its peak in the blood about 30 minutes post-feeding. This primes the mammary gland to produce milk for the next feeding. Prolactin release is highest at night, which supports the importance of nighttime breastfeeding sessions for maintaining supply.

Prolactin stimulates milk synthesis by acting on the mammary epithelial cells. Its levels rise during pregnancy, promoting the proliferation of mammary tissue. However, high levels of progesterone and estrogen inhibit milk secretion despite elevated prolactin. After placental delivery, the drop in these hormones removes this inhibition, allowing prolactin to trigger milk production. Prolactin secretion is stimulated by infant suckling at the nipple, reaching its peak in the blood about 30 minutes post-feeding. This primes the mammary gland to produce milk for the next feeding. Prolactin release is highest at night, which supports the importance of nighttime breastfeeding sessions for maintaining supply.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Mechanism
content: Oxytocin, known as the “let-down” hormone, induces contraction of the myoepithelial cells surrounding alveoli, ejecting stored milk into the ducts. This hormone acts rapidly and can be stimulated not only by infant suckling but also by sensory cues such as seeing, hearing, smelling, or even thinking about the baby. This reflex explains the benefits of mother-infant rooming-in, which facilitates breastfeeding and bonding. Emotional stress can inhibit oxytocin release and impair milk ejection.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Mechanism
content: Initially, prolactin levels are closely linked to nipple stimulation and milk output; however, after several weeks, prolactin levels and milk volume become less tightly linked. Milk secretion will cease if breastfeeding halts due to the accumulation of the feedback inhibitor of lactation (FIL) within alveoli, which signals the cessation of milk production. Milk removal by infant suckling or expression removes FIL, allowing continued synthesis and maintaining supply.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Mechanism
content: Prolactin also benefits the mother by inducing feelings of relaxation and pleasure. Its secretion suppresses the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), leading to diminished secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone. This suppression results in lactational amenorrhea, a natural, temporary form of contraception during breastfeeding.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Pathophysiology
content: One of the primary concerns among mothers is perceived insufficient breast milk supply. As breast milk is essential for a newborn’s well-being, healthcare professionals should evaluate signs of inadequate intake. Such signs include poor weight gain, dry mucous membranes, weak cry, infrequent and hard stools, and decreased urine output. Multiple factors may contribute to low milk supply, such as poor maternal health (eg, anemia), breast tissue abnormalities, retained fetal products, maternal urinary tract infections, and suboptimal feeding techniques. Improving maternal health and establishing effective feeding habits are critical for optimizing milk production and infant nutrition.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Pathophysiology -- Breastfeeding Jaundice
content: Breastfeeding jaundice typically occurs within the first week of life, often caused by insufficient milk intake leading to dehydration and increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. This results in elevated bilirubin levels and subsequent jaundice. Contributing factors include difficulties in breastfeeding or improper latch, which interfere with adequate milk transfer. Infants often show clinical signs of dehydration. Management focuses on ensuring frequent and effective breastfeeding, with support from a lactation consultant to improve technique. Most cases resolve spontaneously by the third week of life.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Pathophysiology -- Breast Milk Jaundice
content: Breast milk jaundice usually begins between 3 and 5 days after birth, peaks around 2 weeks, and lasts for several weeks. It is caused by substances in the breast milk, such as beta-glucuronidase, which increase enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin by deconjugating it in the intestines. Unlike breastfeeding jaundice, affected infants typically gain weight adequately and appear well. This condition generally resolves spontaneously by 12 weeks without treatment, and breastfeeding should be continued throughout.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Pathophysiology -- Milk- or Soy-Induced Colitis
content: Milk- or soy-induced colitis is a hypersensitivity reaction to allergens in breast milk, presenting between 2 and 8 weeks of age with symptoms such as regurgitation, vomiting, and painless bloody stools. Eczema may also be present. It is typically a non-IgE-mediated allergy and commonly occurs alongside soy milk reactions in about 30% of cases. Risk factors include a family history of allergy, eczema, or asthma. Management involves maternal elimination of dairy and soy from the diet, with most cases resolving within 1 year.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Clinical Significance
content: Breastfeeding provides critical protection against a range of diseases, including cardiovascular conditions, atopic disorders, and infections. Additionally, breast milk supports neurodevelopment and reduces the risk of behavioral and developmental disorders in children. [14]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Clinical Significance
content: Breast milk harbors a complex and dynamic microbiome that plays a pivotal role in seeding the infant gut microbiota, promoting immune maturation, and reducing allergy risk. Maternal nutrition, health status, stress levels, and environmental exposures profoundly influence breast milk’s composition, underscoring the value of tailored maternal dietary guidance to optimize lactation outcomes. [15]

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Clinical Significance
content: The rise in breast milk expression and storage, driven by increased maternal workforce participation, necessitates strict hygiene and storage protocols to preserve milk quality and prevent contamination. Stored breast milk remains safe in a refrigerator at 4 °C for up to 5 days and in a freezer at -18 °C for 6 to 12 months, depending on the freezing system. Proper thawing techniques and sterilization of feeding equipment are essential. Contraindications to breastfeeding include the following: Maternal chemotherapy or recent radioactive therapy Human T-cell lymphotropic virus infection or untreated brucellosis Untreated or active tuberculosis Maternal substance abuse (alcohol or illicit drugs) Suspected or untreated maternal HIV infection (with current guidelines reviewing context) An infant with galactosemia In these cases, alternative feeding options should be discussed to ensure infant safety.

title: Physiology, Breast Milk -- Clinical Significance
content: Public health initiatives, including the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative, remain vital to promoting and sustaining breastfeeding globally by providing education, social support, and integration into healthcare systems. By strengthening these initiatives, healthcare systems can secure lasting benefits for maternal and child health across diverse populations.
